0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. Alternate translation: [For the music director] or [For the leader of worship music]

1.note: Here **God of my righteousness** could mean: (1) my righteous God or (2) God who vindicates me. Both options are grammatically possible, and both fit the context well. The following relative clause (verse 1b), which highlights God’s past faithfulness, may suggest that it is God’s righteousness that is in view (hence the UST rendering). You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my God, the righteous one]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. The original word is related to narrowness. Alternate translation: [in trouble] or [when I am oppressed]

2.note: **Son of man** could refer to: (1) the mortality and finitude of his enemies (as opposed to God’s eternal infinitude), (2) important or wealthy men, or (3) the fact that the psalmist is now addressing people rather than God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You men]

2.q: עַד־מֶ֬ה כְבוֹדִ֣⁠י לִ֭⁠כְלִמָּה תֶּאֱהָב֣וּ⁠ן רִ֑יק תְּבַקְשׁ֖וּ כָזָ֣ב
2.note: The psalmist is using the question form to rebuke his enemies. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate these three questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [stop calling glory shame! Stop loving futility! Stop seeking falsehood!]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory** and **shame**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [you consider my glorious deeds as shameful deeds]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **futility** and **falsehood**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [How long will you love vain things? How long will you pursue untrue things?]

3.note: David is using the adjective **godly** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [godly people]

4.note: The implication could be: (1) that the hearers should **tremble** in fear of Yahweh’s punishment for the unfaithful or (2) that if the hearers are angry, they should control themselves and not sin. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Tremble in fear and do not sin] or [Even if you tremble in anger, do not sin]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Consider your thoughts and motives]

The Hebrew root words for speak, **heart**, and **bed** in this verse appear in verses 6 (as “say”), 7, and 8 (as “lie down”) respectively (in the same order). Consider if a similar pattern would create a natural poetic effect in your language.

Here, **be silent** means that the listeners should show self-control and not act on sinful impulses. You could include this information in your translation if it would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and do not act on evil thoughts]

5.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [sacrifices that are righteous]

The words **righteousness** and **trust** form the poetic center of this psalm. **Righteousness** is mentioned in verse 1 and **trust** is the same word translated as “securely” in verse 8. You may wish to explore whether you can reflect this symmetry in a natural way in your language.

6.note: The people asking this are using the question form to make a complaint and an implied request. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate this as an exclamation or plain request. Alternate translation: [No one is showing us good!] or [Please, someone show us good!]

Here, **good** is spoken of as if it were something that someone could **show** to someone else. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Who will do good things for us]

The writer speaks of Yahweh acting favorably towards them as if Yahweh’s face shone a light on them. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Act favorably towards us]
This is a reference to the high priest’s blessing in Numbers 6:25.

7.note: Here the phrase **put joy in my heart** represents that the author’s emotional state is joyful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have made me happy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You have made me glad]

Here, **grain and new wine** represent basic food necessities. An abundance of them represents material prosperity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have a lot of bread and fresh milk] or [they are quite rich]
In Hebrew, this verse uses progressively shorter lines and repeated sounds to create a sense of peaceful rest. Consider if there is a way in your language to create the same sensation.

8.q: בְּ⁠שָׁל֣וֹם יַחְדָּו֮ אֶשְׁכְּבָ֪ה וְ⁠אִ֫ישָׁ֥ן כִּֽי־אַתָּ֣ה יְהוָ֣ה לְ⁠בָדָ֑ד לָ֝⁠בֶ֗טַח תּוֹשִׁיבֵֽ⁠נִי
8.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since you alone, Yahweh, cause me to dwell securely, therefore in peace I will both lie down and sleep.]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Peacefully]
